title: Family office software: which tool fixes which problem?
description: Family office software mapped to the problem each tool fixes: the manual quarterly report, fund PDFs, lagging books, bills and manager diligence.
job: choose a software stack for a family office of 5 to 20 people
verdict: Match tools to problems: platforms target the quarterly report, too manual for 73% of 155 family offices in the Americas.[^1][^64]
Document services such as Arch read the fund PDF flood, which lands in waves after each quarter end.[^31][^59]
Lagging books need a partnership ledger such as FundCount or Eton; QuickBooks Online covers one company per subscription.[^57][^4]
Questionnaire platforms such as DiligenceVault line up fund managers' answers with sources; your investment committee still decides.[^60][^62]
Ask whether each vendor's AI trains on client data: by our count, 10 of 16 say no, Canoe says yes.[^5][^6]

summary: A reporting platform fixes the quarterly report by rolling up custodians and funds, while a partnership ledger fixes lagging books by keeping each entity's accounts.[^9][^4] Document services read fund PDFs and questionnaire platforms line up managers' answers; the plumbing between tools is what breaks.[^31][^60][^2]

recipes.name: 1. Lean office, one or two entities, mostly custodied assets
recipes.when: Pick a general ledger plus light reporting while entities are few, since QuickBooks covers one company per subscription.[^57][^3] Kubera or Asora adds the net-worth view.[^22][^12]
flow: Controller: keep the books in QuickBooks Online Advanced
Controller: tie ledger cash to custodian statements before each report goes out
Ops lead: track net worth in Kubera, or Asora for fuller reporting
Controller: code and route bills in BILL
Second approver: release each payment and confirm any change to wire details
COO: give staff one approved business AI plan, not personal accounts
Principal: review the monthly net-worth report
recipes.cost: QuickBooks Online Advanced is $340 a month, BILL Team $65 per user per month and Kubera Black $2,500 a year.[^3][^29][^22] With two BILL users that is about $8,140 a year by our math; Asora instead of Kubera starts at $900 a month.[^12][^8]

recipes.name: 2. Office of 10 to 20 staff, many entities and private funds
recipes.when: Pick partnership accounting plus a reporting platform once partnerships, trusts and funds multiply.[^4][^9] A UBS survey puts the average family office at 12 staff, and Deloitte's at 15.[^40][^38]
flow: Ops lead: time this quarter's report from close to the principal's desk, as the before number
Controller: run partnership accounting in FundCount or Eton
Ops lead: feed custodian and ledger data into Asora, Aleta or Landytech
Ops lead: trial the reporting platform on one entity before moving the rest
Investment ops analyst: load capital calls and K-1 tax forms through Canoe or Arch
Controller: check every extracted amount and wire detail before it posts
COO: approve which tools may use AI, and on what data terms
recipes.cost: FundCount starts at $35,899 a year for a single family office, Aleta at $1,000 a month, while Eton, Canoe and Arch publish no price.[^4][^18][^25][^5] FundCount plus Aleta comes to about $47,899 a year by our math, before fees, document tools and onboarding.[^4][^18]

recipes.name: 3. Adviser-led office with complex holdings
recipes.when: Pick an institutional reporting platform and outsource the books when the team is thin.[^1][^9] Expertise is the reason to outsource for 87% of family offices surveyed in the Americas.[^1]
flow: COO: have an adviser run the selection, since Simple found that is when selection is structured
Ops lead: implement Addepar or Masttro for reporting
Outsourced accountant: keep the books and send monthly files
Ops lead: connect an approved AI assistant through a read-only MCP link, such as Masttro's
Principal: sign off the quarterly report
recipes.cost: Addepar publishes no price and quotes each deal, and Masttro quotes a flat annual fee.[^15][^11] For scale, published reporting prices start at $900 a month for Asora and $1,000 for Aleta.[^8][^18]

humanRole: A second person approves every payment and every change to payee or wire details. Business email compromise drew 24,768 complaints in 2025, and only investment fraud cost more.[^41]
The controller checks extracted capital call and K-1 figures before they post. Arch builds a person into the loop, with 200+ validation checks.[^31][^24]
The COO sets an AI policy first, approves each tool and keeps sensitive data apart from AI, as offices with formal controls do.[^2] ISO/IEC 42001 is a standard to ask vendors about.[^42][^25]
The ops lead decides whether an AI assistant may only read or may also write. Masttro's MCP link is read-only, while Asora's proposes changes a user confirms.[^43][^44]

ownData.title: What do family office platforms do with your data when their AI reads it?
ownData.intro: By our count, 10 of 16 products say client data never trains their models, Canoe says it fine-tunes its own, and 5 say nothing.[^5][^6] By our count, 6 offer an MCP link for outside assistants, and 5 name an outside model provider.[^43][^23][^45] On 28 Nov 2026 we read each vendor's AI, trust, privacy and pricing pages and logged what it states.[^11][^10]
headers: Does client data train models? (vendor's words)
rows: No explicit statement found; its data pledge covers anonymized analyses[^15][^46]
Leading AI models hosted inside Addepar's environment via Databricks; no provider named[^47]
FAQ says no; privacy policy says its models train on aggregated, anonymized data[^11][^48]
Private AI Service on single-tenant Azure in Switzerland[^49][^11]
Recommends Claude or ChatGPT Team or Enterprise[^6]
Never used to train public language models[^50]

No training line; says private data is not shared with outside systems[^25]

ownData.note: Zavient check of 16 products' public pages, read 28 Nov 2026; the table shows 10, and the counts cover all 16.[^23][^32] Limits: vendor statements only, not contracts, data processing agreements or audit reports, and 'no statement found' does not mean a vendor trains on data.[^48] Box and Salesforce connectors were not checked, and Asset Vantage's AI is not live yet.[^26][^33]

example.input: Illustrative: a capital call notice arrives as a PDF by email. The controller retypes the fund, amount, due date and wire details into the ledger. Then the controller emails the principal for approval.
example.output: After: an extraction tool such as Canoe or Arch reads the fields, and the controller checks them against the fund portal and the last notice.[^31][^5] The ledger posts the entry, and bill pay queues the wire for a second approver.[^24][^10] Any change to wire details stops for a call-back to a known number.[^41]

watchOuts: Building your own system of record: home-built views tend to work, but feeds, reconciliation and history break and hang on one person.[^2] Fix: buy the plumbing and build the view.[^9]

Reading the FAQ, not the contract: Masttro's FAQ rules out AI training, but its privacy policy says models train on anonymized data.[^11][^48] Fix: get data terms in writing, since Canoe's FAQ says client data fine-tunes its models.[^5]

Underinvesting, then patching: of 354 single family offices surveyed, 34% underinvested and 38% only moderately invested in operations technology.[^38] Fix: budget for upgrades, which 51% of family offices surveyed in the Americas call the top long-term risk.[^1]
Skipping implementation cost: vendors typically quote two to four months[^2], and Asora's implementation fee is 25% of the yearly subscription.[^8] Fix: price year one, not the subscription alone.
Underplanning capacity: capacity and implementation came up for 37% of offices and 28% of vendors in Simple's study.[^2] Fix: name an internal owner with time set aside before kickoff.

Personal AI accounts at work: 50% of offices surveyed in the Americas call AI essential, yet split 43% vs 35% on paying for enterprise-grade AI.[^1] Fix: approve a business plan that doesn't train on your data by default.[^52]

faq.q: How much does family office software cost?
faq.a: Published starting prices run from $250 a year for Kubera Essentials to $35,899 a year for FundCount's single family office plan.[^22][^4] Addepar publishes no price and quotes each deal, while Asora starts at $900 a month and Aleta at $1,000.[^15][^8][^18] Most of 146 family offices surveyed spend $100,000 to $500,000 a year on all technology.[^39]

faq.q: What are the alternatives to Addepar?
faq.a: Masttro, Asora, Aleta and Landytech Sesame are the reporting platforms we checked besides Addepar.[^11][^12] Asora and Aleta publish prices from $900 and $1,000 a month, and Landytech from £20k a year plus custodial feeds.[^8][^18][^20]

faq.q: Can we stay on QuickBooks and spreadsheets?
faq.a: Yes, while entities are few: QuickBooks Online Advanced is $340 a month for up to 25 users, but covers one company per subscription.[^57][^3] Of 146 family offices surveyed, 42% still rely on spreadsheets.[^39] With many entities, partnership accounting such as FundCount fits better.[^4]

faq.q: Does the vendor's AI train on our data?
faq.a: Not for most products we checked: by our count, 10 of 16 say client data never trains their models, but Canoe says it does.[^5][^6] Five publish no statement, so ask for the training terms in the contract.[^15][^10]
Two to four months is typical, per vendors' quotes in Simple's study, and longer with much history or many banks.[^2] Aleta says 4 to 8 weeks, and Masttro 12 to 14 weeks.[^18][^11]

faq.q: Do we need a vendor's SOC 2 report?
faq.a: Yes, ask for the System and Organization Controls (SOC) 2 Type 2 report, because it tests whether controls worked over a set period.[^53] Addepar publishes a SOC 3 report covering 1 Sep 2025 to 31 Aug 2026.[^16][^53]

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy the system of record, because vendors warn against building your own and the pattern is 'buy the plumbing, build the view'.[^9][^2] US enterprise AI decision-makers say 76% of their AI use cases were bought in 2025, up from 53% in 2024.[^54]
buyVsBuild.build: Build only the view: a dashboard or assistant on your own data, linked through the MCP connectors Asora, Aleta and Masttro offer.[^44][^18][^43] Keep it narrow: in MIT's study of 52 organizations, internal builds reached deployment about 33% of the time, against about 67% for external partnerships.[^55]

pickElse: Your systems work but don't talk to each other: wire the ledger, bill pay and reporting you have. Of single family offices, 54% keep reporting and 64% financial administration wholly in-house.[^7]

Vendor terms clash with your AI policy: keep sensitive data in the ledger and use a business AI plan that doesn't train by default.[^52][^2] Privacy came up for 39% of vendors and 32% of offices where AI came up, in Simple's study.[^2]
No time to run a platform: outsourced accounting or a managed service fits, a topic 33% of vendors and 24% of offices raised.[^2]
Few entities, simple assets: stay on QuickBooks Online Advanced at $340 a month, or Sage Intacct, which publishes no price and quotes each deal.[^3][^56]

sources.name: RBC Wealth Management and Campden Wealth, North America Family Office Report 2026
sources.what: Survey of 155 single family offices and private multi-family offices across the Americas: 123 in the US, 21 in Canada, 11 elsewhere in the Americas (Figure 1.1). 73% of family offices: investment reporting is too manual (third year running). 50% call AI embedded and essential, 24% disagree; split 43% vs 35% on paying for enterprise-grade AI. Bill pay 81% in-house; financial accounting about 65% in-house (Figure 4.2). Expertise is the reason to outsource for 87%. Failure to upgrade technology is the top long-term risk at 51%. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: Simple, Family Office Software & Technology Report 2026 (PDF)
sources.what: Qualitative study of 41 family offices (31 where AI came up) and 36 vendors. Manual reporting and data plumbing raised by 75% of vendors vs 32% of offices. AI level seen: assistant 55% of offices vs 22% of vendors; task-level 23% vs 47%. Raised by vendors vs offices: capacity and implementation 28% vs 37%; privacy (AI) 39% vs 32% of 31 offices; security 58% vs 46%; outsourcing and managed service 33% vs 24%. "Vendors typically quote two to four months to implement, longer with a lot of history or many banks." Offices with formal AI controls "set a policy first, approve the tools and keep sensitive data apart from what AI can see." Builds of the view tend to work; data plumbing (feeds, reconciliation, history) tends to break, and builds carry key-person dependence. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: MIT NANDA, The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 (Jul 2025)
sources.what: MIT no longer hosts the report (its link now opens the NANDA project page, checked 26 Nov 2026); copy hosted by MLQ.ai. Sample: 52 organizations interviewed, survey of 153 leaders, and 300+ public AI initiatives reviewed. $30-40 billion of enterprise GenAI investment; 95% of organizations are getting zero return; just 5% of integrated AI pilots extract millions in value. Task-specific tools: 60% of organizations evaluated them, 20% piloted, 5% reached production. Over 80% of organizations explored or piloted ChatGPT or Copilot, and nearly 40% report deployment. External partnerships with customized tools reached deployment about 67% of the time vs about 33% for internal builds: 2x as likely, twice the success rate. Only 40% of companies purchased an official LLM subscription; workers at over 90% of companies surveyed use personal AI tools for work. For mission-critical work, 90% of users prefer humans. Enterprises, defined as firms with over $100 million in annual revenue, lead in pilot count but report the lowest pilot-to-scale conversion. Read 26 Nov 2026.

answers.table-2: Published starting prices run from Kubera at $250 a year to FundCount at $35,899 a year, while Addepar, Masttro and Eton publish no price and quote each deal.[^22][^4][^25] Reporting platforms fit consolidation, and FundCount, Eton or Asseta keep multi-entity books.[^9][^4]
answers.table-3: Canoe and Arch read alternatives documents, Box stores them, BILL pays bills, and Affinity or Salesforce Financial Services Cloud tracks relationships.[^5][^31][^33][^10][^35]
answers.table-4: Offices report too much manual work: 73% of 155 family offices surveyed in the Americas call investment reporting too manual, and 81% keep bill pay in-house.[^1]
answers.recipes: Lean offices fit QuickBooks plus Kubera or Asora, multi-entity offices add FundCount or Eton, and adviser-led offices fit Addepar or Masttro.[^3][^4][^11]
answers.human-role: People keep every payment, posting and data-access decision: a second approver releases payments, the controller checks extracted figures, and the COO sets AI data rules.[^41][^2]
answers.example: Illustrative: an extraction tool reads a capital call PDF, the controller checks it, the ledger posts it, and a second approver releases the wire.[^31][^24][^10]
answers.what-goes-wrong: Offices go wrong by building their own system of record, trusting an FAQ over the contract, and skipping implementation cost and capacity.[^2][^48]
answers.buy-or-build: Buy the system of record and build only the view on top, because home-built data plumbing tends to break.[^9][^2]
answers.something-else: Pick neither when the gap is between systems you already own, when vendor data terms clash with your AI policy, or when no one has time to run a platform.[^7][^2]
answers.table-1: Each problem has its own kind of tool: reporting platforms for the quarterly report, document services for fund PDFs, partnership ledgers for the books, and questionnaire platforms for manager diligence.[^1][^31][^4][^60]

offer.heading: Not sure whether you need another platform or better wiring?
offer.body: Often the ledger, bill pay and reporting you own just need to talk to each other. In a free 30-minute call we map your stack, its data flows and each vendor's AI terms. You leave with a pick and a first integration step.

reviews.notes: Read as a family office COO picking a stack for 5 to 20 people. Bottom line gives a pick per pain (reporting, entities, data terms, wiring, timing); recipes size three offices with named roles and dated costs. Recipe 2 had no before-and-after measure; added 'Ops lead: time this quarter's report from close to the principal's desk, as the before number'. FAQ questions were seen in search phrasings and the cluster plan's forum notes (cost, Addepar alternatives, QuickBooks plus spreadsheets, AI training, timing, SOC 2); forums are not cited. Demand: 'family office software' 260 a month at $46.56; 'addepar competitors' 90 at $27.63. Reframe pass: the problem-to-tool table answers what I would ask a vendor first.

Reads on a phone, not IT. Spelled out Amazon Web Services (AWS) in the Addepar row and called ISO 27001 a security certification in the Masttro row. Own-data Addepar cell said 'Frontier models'; now 'Leading AI models hosted inside Addepar's environment'. CRM, MCP, SOC, SEC and LLM are spelled out on first use. Recipe costs cut to two sentences each. Reframe pass: every row names who still signs off.

Wants to try before committing and see the year-one bill. Added Landytech's 14-day trial to its row, and a recipe 2 step to trial the reporting platform on one entity first. Year-one totals by our math are in recipes 1 and 2 ($8,140 and $47,899 a year); the implementation-fee watch-out (Asora 25%) covers the onboarding add-on. No sourced per-entity cost exists beyond Asset Vantage's rupee tiers, so none was added. Reframe pass: vendor claims are labelled as theirs. No consulting firms listed. No changes.

Read as the controller who keeps the books and checks capital calls. Added 'Controller: tie ledger cash to custodian statements before each report goes out' to recipe 1. Human-role bullets keep payment release with a second approver (FBI IC3 business email compromise figures), extracted-figure checks with the controller (Arch's person in the loop), and read-or-write assistant access with the ops lead (Masttro read-only, Asora confirm-first). Reframe pass: the books row matches what I would buy for the ledger.

Steve decides from the title and bottom line: five picks, each under 20 words with two sources. He would distrust a vendor list; the page names software only as products, labels vendor claims and shows where Masttro's FAQ and privacy policy disagree. No Zavient price, per Russell's 26 Nov rule. The offer says what he leaves with: a pick and a first integration step, and frames the call around wiring what he already owns. Reframe pass: no price added.
